ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the circuit diagram, the op-amp is powered by ±10 V. On the left side there is a 100 µF capacitor, whose upper terminal is connected to the +10 V node, and whose lower terminal is connected to the inverting input terminal of the op-amp; switch S is connected in parallel with this capacitor path, so that when the switch is closed, the inverting input node is connected to +10 V. The inverting input node is also connected to −10 V through a 10 kΩ resistor. The op-amp output goes through 470 Ω to the output node Vo, where Z1 and Z2 Zener diodes limit the voltage to ground, therefore Vo is clamped to +5 V or −5 V. Vo is also fed back through a 4 kΩ resistor to the non-inverting input terminal of the op-amp, and the non-inverting input terminal is then connected to ground through 1 kΩ, forming a feedback voltage divider. Reasoning: When switch S is initially closed, the capacitor is short-circuited, and the initial voltage at the inverting input terminal is V−(0)=+10 V. After t=0 the switch opens, and the inverting input terminal changes toward −10 V through the 10 kΩ resistor, with time constant τ=RC=10 kΩ×100 µF=1 s. Therefore V−(t)=−10+(10−(−10))e^(−t/τ)=−10+20e^(−t). Initially V−=+10 V, greater than the possible voltage at the non-inverting terminal, therefore the op-amp output is negatively saturated, and Vo is clamped at −5 V. At this time the non-inverting input terminal obtains V+=−5×1/(4+1)=−1 V from voltage division by 4 kΩ and 1 kΩ. The output changes state when V− drops to this threshold: −10+20e^(−t)=−1, so 20e^(−t)=9, e^(−t)=9/20=0.45, t=−ln(0.45)≈0.798 s≈0.8 s.
